blocks.text: A plain sorted linked list has O(1) insertion at a known point but O(n) search, since you can only walk one node at a time from the head. A skip list fixes this by adding extra express lane layers on top of a sorted linked list, so search can skip over many elements at once, achieving O(log n) EXPECTED search, insert, and delete, all without any rotations or rebalancing logic at all, unlike AVL or Red Black trees.

Skip lists trade a hard, worst case O(log n) guarantee (what AVL or Red Black trees provide via strict invariants and rotations) for a much simpler implementation with an EXPECTED O(log n) bound backed by randomization. This tradeoff is exactly why Redis chose skip lists for its sorted set implementation.

blocks.caption: Level 0 contains every element in sorted order. Each level above contains a randomly chosen subset of the elements below it, forming progressively sparser express lanes.
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406865740-174140849.png

Multiple levels of linked lists are stacked on top of each other. Level 0 contains every element in sorted order, exactly like a normal sorted linked list. Each level above it contains a randomly chosen SUBSET of the elements on the level below, so higher levels are progressively sparser and let a search jump over larger stretches of the list.

A node's "height," how many levels it appears on, is chosen randomly at insertion time, typically by flipping a fair coin repeatedly: start the new node at level 0, and for as long as the coin comes up heads, promote it to one level higher. This gives roughly half as many nodes at each successive level, exactly the geometric shape that produces logarithmic search depth on average.

There is no explicit balancing step anywhere in a skip list, no rotations, no recoloring, nothing. The probabilistic level assignment described above is entirely what keeps the structure balanced ON AVERAGE, in expectation, purely as a side effect of how new nodes are randomly promoted to higher levels.

This is the single biggest practical advantage over AVL or Red Black trees: a correct skip list implementation is dramatically simpler to write and to reason about under concurrent modification, since there is no invariant that a partial update could ever leave in a genuinely broken state, only a temporarily suboptimal one.

blocks.caption: Search starts at the highest level and moves right as far as possible before dropping down one level, repeating until level 0 is reached.
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406865740-999541313.png

Start at the top left corner, the highest level's head pointer. Move RIGHT as long as the next node's value is less than the target. When you cannot move right anymore without overshooting past the target, drop DOWN one level and repeat the same rightward scan. Continue until level 0 is reached, where the target is either found directly or confirmed absent.

Every level skipped over during this descent represents work that a plain linked list would have had to do one node at a time. This is the entire value proposition of the extra levels: they let the search commit to large jumps early and only slow down to fine grained, single step movement once it is close to the target.

Searching for value 7 in a 3 level skip list containing 1, 3, 5, 7, 9: starting at the level 2 head, the express lane goes directly 1 to 9. Since 9 is greater than 7, drop down to level 1 without moving right. At level 1, the lane goes 1 to 5 to 9. Move right to 5 (5 is less than 7), then the next node is 9, which is greater than 7, so drop down to level 0. At level 0, move right from 5 to 7, and 7 matches the target, found.

Contrast this with a plain sorted linked list, which would have walked 1, 3, 5, 7 one node at a time, four steps versus the skip list's two express lane jumps plus one final step, a small example, but the gap widens dramatically as the list grows larger.

Insertion follows the same search pattern first: walk down from the top level exactly as in search, but this time RECORD, at every level, the last node visited before dropping down, these recorded nodes are exactly the ones whose forward pointers will need to be spliced around the new node.

Once the level 0 insertion point is found, generate a random level for the new node using the same coin flip technique described earlier. Then splice the new node into every level up to its randomly chosen height, using the recorded nodes from the search phase to relink the forward pointers at each of those levels.

Search, insert, and delete are all O(log n) in EXPECTATION, meaning on average across random level assignments, not as a worst case guarantee. It is worth stating this distinction clearly: an AVL or Red Black tree GUARANTEES O(log n) height no matter what, a skip list only achieves O(log n) height with high probability given proper randomization.

In an extremely unlikely worst case, poor random level assignments could produce a skip list that degrades toward O(n), effectively behaving like a plain linked list, but this probability shrinks exponentially as more nodes are inserted, making it a non issue in practice for any reasonable implementation with a proper random number generator.

blocks.text: This simplicity is exactly why skip lists back Redis sorted sets and appear inside LevelDB and RocksDB style storage engines, correctness under concurrent access matters enormously in those systems, and a structure with no rebalancing step at all is easier to get right under concurrent modification than a tree requiring atomic multi node rotations.

Forgetting to update ALL levels a node participates in during insert or delete, not just level 0, leaves the higher express lanes pointing at stale or incorrect nodes, silently corrupting future searches that use those lanes.

Choosing a poor probability for the coin flip: the standard choice is 0.5, giving roughly half as many nodes at each level, a probability too close to 0 or 1 either produces too few levels (degrading toward a plain linked list) or too many nearly empty levels (wasting memory without meaningfully improving search).

Off by one errors in the "move right while less than target" condition: using less than or equal instead of strictly less than can cause the search to overshoot past the target before dropping down, missing the correct insertion or search point.

This is primarily a system design and algorithm knowledge topic. It rarely appears as a raw coding problem the way AVL or Red Black trees occasionally do, but "Design Skiplist" does exist as a direct LeetCode style implementation exercise, and skip lists are a genuinely common system design interview topic when discussing how Redis sorted sets work internally.

Can you trace a search, including exactly when the algorithm drops down a level versus continues moving right?
Can you explain why skip lists are preferred over balanced trees in systems like Redis specifically because of concurrent modification behavior?

description: Learn how a skip list uses randomized express lane levels on top of a sorted linked list to achieve expected O(log n) search without any rotations
